title: Nontransitive dice and fair decks
sections: For independent uniform draws from decks of m and n physical cards, each of the mn card pairs is equally likely. A win probability is the number of winning physical pairs divided by mn. Repeated values remain separate cards. Replacement restores the same probabilities in each round.

A strict cycle exists: A=(2,4,9), B=(1,6,8), C=(3,5,7) give P(A>B)=P(B>C)=P(C>A)=5/9. Thus pairwise advantage need not be transitive, and deck totals do not determine it. Duplicating every card equally preserves probabilities; duplicating only selected cards need not.

Small-deck limit: Three cards per deck is the minimum for a strict three-way majority cycle among equal-size fair decks with no values shared across decks. For two-card decks, writing each in nondecreasing order, one wins more than half the pairs exactly when both its corresponding values are larger. That relation is transitive. One-card comparisons are transitive too.

When 1–9 are used once in three three-card decks, all three cyclic advantages cannot be at least 6/9. A finite winner-only run also cannot establish with certainty which of the original decks has the advantage: every finite win/loss sequence has positive probability under either direction.
K–1: Compare cards and organize all pairs; contrast pair counts with a six-round game. Fractions are optional.
Grades 2–3: Construct cycles, track multiplicity, and reason about what a finite experiment can establish.
Grades 4–5: Certify exact probabilities and complete searches, then prove small-deck and strong-cycle obstructions.

The launch demonstrates one draw and its recorded winner, leaving the complete pair collection open. Games provide data; a proposed cycle is a conjecture until all relevant pairs are counted. Order arguments establish impossibility beyond the tested examples.
